articles.title: OpenAI Just Hired Uber India's Boss to Run Its Second-Biggest Market. It's Not Messing Around.
articles.excerpt: Prabhjeet Singh, an IIT-IIM alumnus who spent a decade building Uber across South Asia, will become OpenAI's most senior leader in India as the company races to convert ChatGPT's consumer popularity into institutional muscle.
articles.image_caption: The 2026 AI Impact Summit plenary session in New Delhi, where India unveiled its sovereign AI ambitions
articles.nri_angle: India-origin tech professionals worldwide are watching as the AI industry's centre of gravity shifts toward India, where OpenAI's aggressive hiring of IIT-IIM alumni signals career opportunities beyond Silicon Valley.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Adani Just Committed $2.1 Billion to Turn Six Indian Airports Into Small Cities. Mumbai Gets the Biggest Share.
articles.excerpt: The plan calls for hotels, offices, retail, and entertainment districts spanning 655 acres across Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Lucknow, Jaipur, and Guwahati — modelled on Changi, Schiphol, and Incheon.
articles.image_caption: The interior of Mumbai's international terminal, which will anchor Adani's largest airport city investment
articles.nri_angle: For India's 32 million-strong diaspora, airports are the first and last impression of the country — Adani's Changi-inspired plan promises the kind of seamless arrival experience NRIs have long wished for.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Rubio Says Trump Is Coming to India. The Trade Deal, He Says, Is 'on the Last Inches.'
articles.excerpt: In separate White House interviews, America's top diplomat and its envoy to India described the relationship as 'stronger than ever' — and signalled a presidential visit early next year.
articles.image_caption: Prime Minister Narendra Modi meets President Donald Trump at the White House in Washington DC, February 2025
articles.nri_angle: Trade deal terms, H-1B visa policy, and the diplomatic temperature all directly shape the professional and economic lives of 5.1 million Indian Americans.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Is Selling Its Deadliest Weapons to the Gulf. The UAE Is First in Line.
articles.excerpt: After the Iran war exposed the Gulf's dependence on American military hardware, the UAE is in talks to buy India's supersonic BrahMos missile and its AI-powered Akashteer air defence system — a deal that would reshape defence alignments across the Middle East.
articles.image_caption: A BrahMos supersonic cruise missile on display at a DRDO exhibition in India
articles.nri_angle: More than 3.5 million Indians live in the UAE — Gulf security directly affects their safety, livelihoods, and the remittance corridor that sends billions home annually.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Iran Just Claimed Ownership of the World's Most Important Shipping Lane. India Has 200,000 Reasons to Worry.
articles.excerpt: A second tanker was hit on Saturday as Tehran demands ships get Iranian permits to cross the Strait of Hormuz, and Washington warns 'violence will be met with violence.' For India, whose seafarers and oil supply depend on the strait, the ceasefire that was supposed to fix everything is falling apart.
articles.image_caption: US Navy ships transit the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway Iran now claims to control
articles.nri_angle: Over 200,000 Indian seafarers work on international vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz — their safety is directly at stake as Iran asserts control over the shipping lane that also carries most of India's crude oil imports.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Man Who Inspired '3 Idiots' Is About to Join India's Gen Z Revolt. He Says He'll Stop Eating Until the Government Listens.
articles.excerpt: Sonam Wangchuk will begin an indefinite hunger strike at Delhi's Jantar Mantar on Sunday, aligning with the Cockroach Janta Party — a meme-born movement that has CNN, the Wall Street Journal, and 20 million Instagram followers paying attention to India's exam crisis.
articles.image_caption: Sonam Wangchuk, the Ladakhi engineer and climate activist who inspired the film 3 Idiots
articles.nri_angle: The NEET exam crisis undermines the credentials that propelled millions of diaspora professionals into careers abroad, while the CJP's founder is himself a US-educated Indian who returned to lead the movement.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Year Ago, India and Canada Were Expelling Each Other's Diplomats. Now Modi Has Been Invited to Ottawa.
articles.excerpt: Four meetings in under a year, a defence dialogue, a $2.6 billion uranium deal, and a trade target of $50 billion by 2030 — the India-Canada reset is moving at a pace that would have been unthinkable during the Khalistan crisis.
articles.image_caption: Prime Minister Narendra Modi meets Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in Evian, France
articles.nri_angle: For 1.8 million Indians in Canada, the diplomatic thaw means restored consular services, smoother visa processing, and a safer environment after years of Khalistan-related tensions.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Every Forecaster Is Saying the Same Thing: India Is Slowing Down. Here Is Why.
articles.excerpt: S&P, UBS, HDFC Bank, and the RBI all project growth between 6.2% and 6.7% for FY27 — down from 7.7% — as energy stress, a record monsoon deficit, and softening business confidence converge on the world's fastest-growing major economy.
articles.image_caption: The Bombay Stock Exchange building in Mumbai, hub of India's equity markets
articles.nri_angle: NRI investors with equity, bond, and FCNR holdings in India face a shifting landscape as rate hikes, a weakening rupee, and softer corporate earnings rewrite the calculus on where to park overseas savings.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: He Built a Credit-Card App With $1 Million of His Own Money. Now He Runs WhatsApp for 3 Billion People.
articles.excerpt: Meta tapped CRED founder Kunal Shah to lead its biggest messaging platform, invested $900 million in his startup, and handed an Indian entrepreneur the keys to one of the world's most-used products.
articles.image_caption: Kunal Shah, founder of CRED, has been appointed as WhatsApp's new global head by Meta
articles.nri_angle: An Indian entrepreneur who built his companies in India — not through a Western corporate ladder — now runs the messaging app that millions of NRIs rely on daily to stay connected with family and community.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Most Ambitious Trade Deal Goes Live on July 15. If You Work in the UK, Read This.
articles.excerpt: The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement eliminates tariffs on 99 per cent of Indian exports, exempts 75,000 Indian professionals from British social security payments, and aims to double bilateral trade to $120 billion by 2030.
articles.image_caption: Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal has led India's preparations for the CETA rollout on July 15
articles.nri_angle: The deal directly benefits 75,000 Indian professionals in the UK with a five-year exemption from British social security contributions and opens streamlined entry for Indian workers — reshaping the economic terms under which NRIs in Britain live and work.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Oil Just Had Its Worst Week Since the War Began. India — the World's Third-Largest Importer — Hasn't Cut Fuel Prices by a Single Rupee.
articles.excerpt: Brent crashed 11% to $72, Saudi Aramco restarted its biggest terminal, and an RBI official says $70 oil could push India back to 7% growth. But petrol and diesel remain ₹7.50 a litre above pre-war levels.
articles.image_caption: An oil tanker at sea in the waters near the Middle East
articles.nri_angle: Lower crude prices ease pressure on India's current account, strengthen the rupee, and improve the growth outlook — all of which directly affect the value of NRI remittances, investments, and the cost of flights and goods sent home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America Just Decided Who Gets to Use the World's Most Powerful AI. India Had to Ask Not to Be Left Out.
articles.excerpt: Washington restricted Anthropic's Fable 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 over security fears. India's top tech official flew to the Pax Silica Summit to secure a promise: trusted partners won't face 'abrupt cutoffs.'
articles.image_caption: Server racks inside a data centre, the physical infrastructure powering frontier AI models
articles.nri_angle: Indian tech workers in the US are building with these restricted AI models daily, while India's $250-billion IT services industry — the diaspora's biggest employment pipeline — is betting its next growth cycle on uninterrupted access to frontier AI.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Iran Is Offering India $4-a-Barrel Discounts on Crude. So Far, India Isn't Biting.
articles.excerpt: Middlemen from Singapore and Dubai are flooding Indian refiners with offers of cheap Iranian oil after Washington's 60-day sanctions waiver — but full tanks and unclear payment channels are keeping buyers on the sidelines.
articles.image_caption: A crude oil tanker at sea — the kind of vessel now at the centre of renewed Iran-India energy trade talks
articles.nri_angle: Energy prices directly affect the cost of cooking gas, petrol and airline tickets for millions of Indians and shape the inflation outlook that NRIs watch when sending remittances or investing back home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Russia Now Supplies More Than Half of India's Oil. Washington Says the Waiver That Made It Possible Is Over.
articles.excerpt: Record Russian crude imports hit 2.66 million barrels a day in June while Iran's petroleum minister lands in Delhi with a rival offer — and the US signals both doors could close.
articles.image_caption: An oil refinery processing crude petroleum
articles.nri_angle: A weaker rupee from higher energy costs erodes the purchasing power of family remittances, raises airfares and food prices, and puts the India-US trade deal — critical to diaspora professionals — on shakier ground.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: He Left Hyderabad With $8. His Company Just Put $1 Billion Back Into India — and Wants to Buy a Whole Bank.
articles.excerpt: Prem Watsa's Fairfax snapped up nearly a billion dollars of Indian government bonds in a single day. The real target is IDBI Bank, in what could be India's biggest bank privatisation ever.
articles.image_caption: Prem Watsa, founder and chairman of Fairfax Financial Holdings
articles.nri_angle: A Hyderabad-born IIT Madras graduate who built a Canadian financial empire is now making the largest foreign bid for an Indian bank — a powerful symbol of the diaspora's shift from sending remittances to deploying serious capital back home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Amazon Just Raised Its India Bet to $48 Billion. Most of the New Money Is Going to AI.
articles.excerpt: CEO Andy Jassy met Modi in New Delhi and announced $13 billion in fresh capital for data centres in Mumbai and Hyderabad — the latest move in a hyperscaler arms race that is turning India into a global AI hub.
articles.image_caption: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, who met PM Modi in New Delhi to announce the investment
articles.nri_angle: Amazon employs hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin workers globally and plans to support 3.8 million jobs in India by 2030, creating new career bridges for NRIs in cloud and AI.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Washington Just Fined an Indian Immigration Lawyer $255,000 for Filing Cookie-Cutter Asylum Claims. That's Only Half the Story.
articles.excerpt: In the same week, a separate ring of Indian nationals pleaded guilty to staging armed robberies at convenience stores so fake 'victims' could apply for U visas. Both cases signal a new phase in the crackdown on immigration fraud.
articles.image_caption: The John Joseph Moakley United States Courthouse in Boston, where the staged robbery visa fraud case was heard
articles.nri_angle: The crackdown directly affects Indian nationals in the US asylum system and raises concerns that high-profile fraud cases could invite broader scrutiny on all Indian visa applicants.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America Just Bombed Iran Again. The Trigger Was a Drone Hitting a Ship in the World's Most Important Oil Lane.
articles.excerpt: Nine days after a ceasefire, the US struck Iranian missile, drone and radar sites in retaliation for an attack on a cargo vessel crossing the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint where thousands of Indian sailors work and through which a fifth of the world's oil flows. A UN evacuation of stranded crews is on hold.
articles.image_caption: A satellite view of the Strait of Hormuz, the oil chokepoint where the US struck Iran after a drone hit a cargo ship
articles.nri_angle: The Strait of Hormuz is where thousands of Indian seafarers work and through which most of India's imported crude and cooking gas flows, so a US strike on Iran there directly threatens Indian crews stranded at sea, the oil-import bill behind India's fuel prices, and the millions of Gulf-based NRIs whose livelihoods and remittances depend on a stable region.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Says a Trade Deal With America Is 'Done.' It Just Won't Switch It On Until the Tariffs Favour India.
articles.excerpt: After two days of talks with Washington's trade chief in New Delhi, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal says the framework is agreed — but the pact stays in the drawer until the US guarantees India a lower tariff than Vietnam, Bangladesh and the rest. A July 24 deadline is now ticking against both sides.
articles.image_caption: Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who says the India-US trade pact is agreed but awaits a tariff edge
articles.nri_angle: A US-India trade pact sits squarely on the corridor the diaspora lives on — the importers, IT-services firms, diaspora-founded startups and the 330,000-plus Indian students who move goods, software and capital between the two economies — so whether the deal switches on, and on what tariff terms, directly shapes the commercial world Indian-Americans operate in.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Hyderabad Just Named a Road After Donald Trump. The Backlash Came From an Unexpected Direction.
articles.excerpt: A Congress-run state put the US President's name on a street beside the American consulate, in the heart of a financial district ringed by Microsoft, Google and Amazon. The sharpest objection came not from Trump's critics but from Narendra Modi's own party, which called it 'hypocrisy.'
articles.image_caption: Hyderabad's Financial District, home to US tech offices and the consulate, where a road was renamed Donald Trump Avenue
articles.nri_angle: The road sits at the centre of the US-India tech corridor the diaspora is built on — the Microsoft/Google/Amazon engineering hub in Hyderabad that feeds H-1B and Silicon Valley talent — and the cross-party fight over honouring Trump shows Indian-Americans that backing the American alliance is no longer a settled consensus back home but a live political fault line.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Diaspora Used to Send Money Home. Now It's Investing in India — and GIFT City Is the New Address.
articles.excerpt: A digital wealth platform built for NRIs just doubled its inflows in two months, almost all of it fresh money wired in from abroad. It is the clearest sign yet of a quiet shift: overseas Indians are no longer just remitting to family — they are building India into a global portfolio, and Gujarat's tax-neutral finance city is where they are doing it.
articles.image_caption: GIFT City in Gandhinagar, Gujarat — India's tax-neutral international financial centre, now a hub for NRI investment
articles.nri_angle: Overseas Indians are shifting from sending remittances to actively building India into a global investment portfolio — wiring fresh dollars abroad into GIFT City mutual funds, fixed deposits and soon Nifty derivatives — giving NRIs in the Gulf, US and UK a tax-efficient, foreign-currency way to take a growth stake in India rather than treating it only as a place to support family.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: For a Generation, 'Study Abroad' Meant America, Canada, Britain or Australia. That Era Is Quietly Ending.
articles.excerpt: Indian student numbers in the US fell at their sharpest pace in a decade this year, Canada's intake has collapsed, and Australia has slapped India with its highest tier of visa scrutiny. As the traditional Big Four pull up the drawbridge, a new map of where India's young go to learn — and to build a future — is taking shape.
articles.image_caption: International students on a university campus; Indian enrolment in the traditional Big Four destinations is declining
articles.nri_angle: The student pipeline is the diaspora's renewal mechanism, and as the Big Four — the US, Canada, UK and Australia — tighten visas and caps, the next generation of overseas Indians is being redirected toward Germany, Ireland and the UAE, meaning a thinner inflow of young arrivals to refresh the established diaspora's community institutions, businesses and emerging political voice in the traditional destinations.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Says Your Passport Doesn't Prove You're a Citizen. The Diaspora Should Read the Fine Print.
articles.excerpt: A single line from a government official — a passport is a travel document, not proof of citizenship — has set off a national argument about who counts as Indian. Shashi Tharoor has stepped in with a fix, and for NRIs and OCI holders, the stakes are quietly personal.
articles.image_caption: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor, who has urged a 'durable' legal status for Indians abroad amid the passport-citizenship debate
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs and the millions holding OCI cards, India's clarification that a passport is not proof of citizenship — and Tharoor's reminder that OCI is 'only a lifetime visa' that can be revoked — underscores how thin their formal legal tie to India really is, making the call for a durable dual-citizenship formula a directly personal stake for the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Is the World's Cheapest Place to Work Remotely. It Still Won't Give Digital Nomads a Visa.
articles.excerpt: A third of Indian travellers now want to work from a hillside or a beach, a Himalayan village has reinvented itself for laptops, and dozens of countries are courting Indian remote workers. The one place that hasn't built a door for them is India itself.
articles.image_caption: A remote worker on a laptop; India ranks as the world's most affordable base for digital nomads
articles.nri_angle: The digital nomad is a new kind of NRI — moving fluidly between countries on an Indian salary rather than emigrating for good — and as H-1B and student-to-work routes tighten, dozens of nomad-visa programmes (Estonia, UAE, Spain, Thailand and more) offer the Indian diaspora a flexible, lower-commitment way to live abroad without giving up their Indian base, even as India itself, the world's cheapest nomad destination, still offers no such visa.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Texas Is Building Its Own H-1B Crackdown — and Indian Workers Are Caught in the Middle
articles.excerpt: A state has no power to run the H-1B program. That hasn't stopped Texas. With 'ghost office' probes, subpoenas to employers, a legislative review and a freeze on state hiring that runs to 2027, the country's H-1B fight now has a second front — one squarely aimed at the industry Indians dominate.
articles.image_caption: Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who has frozen new H-1B petitions by state agencies and universities through May 2027
articles.nri_angle: Indians receive roughly 70% of H-1B visas, so Texas's new state-level enforcement — 'ghost office' probes, AG subpoenas, a legislative review and a freeze on state and university hiring through May 2027 — lands first on Indian tech workers, researchers and physicians in the booming Austin-Dallas-Houston diaspora corridors, and threatens to spread a 'Texans first' patchwork of local restrictions on top of an already tightening federal H-1B system.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Joins 34 Nations in Washington to Pick a Side in the Coming AI Order
articles.excerpt: At the second Pax Silica Summit, 35 countries signed a Joint Statement on AI Opportunity — a 'build first' manifesto for chips, compute and critical minerals. For a diaspora that already runs much of Silicon Valley, India's seat at the table is more than symbolic.
articles.image_caption: A semiconductor wafer; India joined 34 nations in signing the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity at the Pax Silica Summit
articles.nri_angle: India joining 34 nations in signing the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity at the Pax Silica Summit deepens a US-India technology axis that runs straight through the diaspora — Indian-origin leaders run Google, Microsoft and major chip and cloud firms, and Indian engineers fill design teams from Silicon Valley to Bengaluru — promising more cross-border chip investment and research ties, a potential counterweight to immigration headwinds, but also pulling Indian talent into a more openly contested geopolitical project.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Monsoon Is Running 43% Short, and 315 Districts Are Now on a Government Watch List
articles.excerpt: With June rains the weakest in years and El Nino threatening the driest season in over a decade, Delhi has drawn up emergency plans for the farm belt. For a diaspora that watches food prices and the rupee from afar, the stakes run from the dinner table to the markets.
articles.image_caption: Farmland during the monsoon in India; a weak 2026 season has put 315 districts on a government contingency watch list
articles.nri_angle: A weak 2026 monsoon — running 43% below average with 315 farm districts now on a government watch list — threatens food inflation and rural incomes that directly touch the diaspora, whose remittances, Indian property and market investments, and family ties back home all rise and fall with the rains, and which feeds straight into the rupee pressure behind the RBI's new NRI deposit scheme.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ambani's Jio Just Filed for What Could Be India's Biggest IPO Ever. The Regulator Is Already Asking Questions.
articles.excerpt: Jio Platforms wants to raise about Rs 35,000 crore in an all-fresh share issue that could value the digital giant near $131 billion. SEBI has sought clarifications on the draft prospectus — a routine step before one of three mega-listings set to test the market this year.
articles.image_caption: Reliance chairman Mukesh Ambani, whose Jio Platforms has filed for what could be India's largest-ever IPO
articles.nri_angle: Jio Platforms' filing for what could be India's largest-ever IPO — an all-fresh Rs 35,000 crore issue valuing the business near $131 billion — gives the global diaspora a rare chance to own a stake in the network that carries their calls home and powers India's digital economy, at a moment when three mega-listings test whether the market can absorb them.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: After Nearly Two Years, India Reopens Its Doors to Bangladeshi Tourists
articles.excerpt: From June 28, Bangladeshis can once again apply for Indian tourist visas at five centres across the country, ending a suspension that began amid the 2024 upheaval. The thaw is the clearest sign yet that ties between the two neighbours are mending.
articles.image_caption: Tourists at the Taj Mahal in Agra. India will resume issuing tourist visas to Bangladeshi nationals from June 28, 2026, ending a nearly two-year suspension.
articles.nri_angle: India's decision to resume tourist visas for Bangladeshi nationals from June 28, after a nearly two-year suspension, signals a thawing of relations that resonates across the eastern subcontinent's diaspora — families straddling the India-Bangladesh frontier, and the large Bangladeshi-origin communities in Britain, the US, Canada and the Gulf with relatives on both sides, can again plan the cross-border visits for weddings, funerals and reunions that had been tangled in geopolitics since 2024.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Europe Is Living Through Its Worst Heatwave on Record. Millions of Indians Live Right In It.
articles.excerpt: Britain, France and Switzerland have all broken June temperature records as a 'killer' heatwave scientists link to climate change grips the continent. With dozens dead and code-red alerts from London to the Netherlands, the diaspora is feeling the heat too.
articles.image_caption: A Copernicus Sentinel-3 satellite image of southern Europe during an exceptional heatwave. Western Europe is enduring its worst recorded heatwave, with the UK, France and Switzerland breaking June temperature records in late June 2026.
articles.nri_angle: Europe's worst recorded heatwave is the weather outside the windows of millions of Indians who now call the continent home — roughly two million people of Indian origin in the UK alone, plus hundreds of thousands across France, Germany, Italy and the Netherlands — many living in homes built for a cool climate, without air conditioning, leaving elderly relatives, students in un-air-conditioned exam halls and outdoor workers acutely exposed as records fall and code-red alerts spread.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: 200 Indian Americans Just Walked Into 125 Congressional Offices in a Single Day
articles.excerpt: The fourth annual FIIDS Capitol Hill Day on June 23 was the largest diaspora advocacy push yet — delegates from 25 states pressed lawmakers on US-India ties, high-skilled immigration and critical minerals, while Indian American Congressmen urged the community to stop watching from the sidelines and run for office.
articles.image_caption: The United States Capitol. Nearly 200 Indian American delegates visited more than 125 Congressional offices during the fourth annual FIIDS Capitol Hill Day on June 23, 2026
articles.nri_angle: The fourth annual FIIDS Capitol Hill Day on June 23, 2026 — nearly 200 Indian American delegates from 25 states working more than 125 Congressional offices in a single day — marks the diaspora's largest and most organised legislative advocacy push yet, pressing Washington on US-India ties, high-skilled immigration reform and critical minerals, while Indian American lawmakers urged the community to convert its economic weight into political power by running for office.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Australia's Under-16 Social Media Ban Isn't Working Yet — and Indian-Australian Families Have a Big Stake in What Happens Next
articles.excerpt: Six months after the world-first ban took effect, a new study finds teen use is little changed, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says he will toughen enforcement. With India now Australia's single largest source of migrants, the policy lands squarely on hundreds of thousands of diaspora households raising teenagers.
articles.image_caption: Australia's world-first ban bars under-16s from holding accounts on major social media platforms. A new study finds teen use is little changed six months in
articles.nri_angle: Six months after Australia's world-first ban on under-16 social media accounts, a new BMJ study finds teen use is little changed and PM Albanese is moving to toughen enforcement — a debate that lands directly on the diaspora, since India is now Australia's single largest source of migrants (971,020 India-born, up 55,000 in a year), meaning hundreds of thousands of Indian-Australian households raising teenagers have a direct stake in whether the law works and in the privacy trade-offs of stricter age checks.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Just Raised Passport Fees for the First Time in Years. Here's the New Price List.
articles.excerpt: From July 1, a basic adult passport jumps from Rs 1,500 to Rs 2,500 and a lost-passport replacement under Tatkal can run to Rs 8,500. The Ministry of External Affairs has revised charges across every category, from minors to police clearance certificates.
articles.image_caption: An Indian passport. The Ministry of External Affairs has raised passport fees across all categories effective July 1, 2026
articles.nri_angle: India is raising passport fees across every category from July 1, 2026 — a basic adult passport rises to Rs 2,500 and a lost-passport Tatkal replacement to as much as Rs 8,500 — and because Indian missions abroad benchmark consular fees to the domestic schedule, NRIs renewing or replacing passports overseas should expect higher charges and can lock in the old rate by filing before July 1.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: You Can Now Clear Immigration in Varanasi and Fly to the World Through Delhi Without Touching Your Bags
articles.excerpt: Air India's new 'Easy Connect' flights, launching from Varanasi on June 25, let travellers from smaller Indian cities check baggage through to their final destination and complete international immigration at their home airport. A phased rollout to more Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities is planned.
articles.image_caption: An Air India aircraft. The airline's new 'Easy Connect' flights launch from Varanasi under the government's hub-and-spoke model
articles.nri_angle: Air India's new 'Easy Connect' hub-and-spoke flights, launching from Varanasi on June 25 with a phased rollout to more Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, let travellers check baggage through to their final destination and clear international immigration at their home airport — a direct win for the large share of the diaspora whose roots are in smaller Indian cities and who have long endured collecting and re-checking bags and a second immigration queue at Delhi mid-journey.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Is Quietly Offering Its Diaspora a Rare Deal: Park Dollars Home, Earn Almost Like Stocks
articles.excerpt: The RBI is swallowing the currency-hedging cost on new FCNR(B) deposits, pushing rates to 6-7%. With loans now allowed against those deposits through GIFT City, returns could climb toward double digits — and analysts expect tens of billions of NRI dollars to follow.
articles.image_caption: The Reserve Bank of India headquarters in Mumbai, which is absorbing the hedging cost on new FCNR(B) diaspora deposits
articles.nri_angle: The RBI is absorbing the currency-hedging cost on new three-to-five-year FCNR(B) deposits, pushing dollar rates for non-resident Indians to 6-7% with no rupee risk — and with loans now permitted against those deposits through GIFT City, leveraged returns could approach 12-15%, making 'sending money home' a genuinely competitive investment for the world's 35-million-strong Indian diaspora rather than an act of sentiment.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's UAE Embassy Is Hitting Pause on Passports and Visas for Five Days. Here's What 4 Million Indians Need to Know.
articles.excerpt: Regular consular services in the UAE shut from June 26 to June 30 as the mission swaps outsourcing partners. From July 1, a new operator, Al Hind Tours and Travel, takes over passport, visa and attestation work.
articles.image_caption: The Abu Dhabi skyline; the Indian Embassy is pausing regular passport, visa and consular services across the UAE from June 26 to 30 during a provider switch
articles.nri_angle: Regular Indian passport, visa, attestation and consular services across the UAE — home to the world's largest Indian diaspora community of about 4.4 million — are paused from June 26 to 30 as the embassy switches its outsourced provider from BLS/SGIVS to Al Hind Tours and Travel, meaning non-emergency applicants should file before June 26 or wait until July 1, while already-submitted applications and genuine emergencies remain covered.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Shafali Verma Lights Up Old Trafford as India Keep Their World Cup Alive
articles.excerpt: A 53 off 34 from the returning opener powered a five-wicket win over Bangladesh in Manchester. Now a Sunday showdown with Australia at Lord's will decide India's semifinal fate.
articles.image_caption: Old Trafford in Manchester, where India beat Bangladesh by five wickets to keep their T20 World Cup campaign alive
articles.nri_angle: The Women's T20 World Cup is being staged in England, home to roughly two million people of Indian origin, turning grounds like Old Trafford into diaspora gathering points; India's five-wicket win over Bangladesh and Shafali Verma's match-winning half-century keep the reigning ODI champions on course for a semifinal in front of their largest overseas fanbase, with a defining clash against Australia at Lord's on Sunday.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: 'If You Don't Have a Seat at the Table, You're on the Menu': The Diaspora's Loudest Year in Washington
articles.excerpt: Nearly 200 Indian-American delegates fanned out across Capitol Hill this week as lawmakers urged the community to run for office — a civic surge sharpened by rising anti-Hindu and anti-India hate.
articles.image_caption: The US Capitol, where nearly 200 Indian-American delegates lobbied more than 125 Congressional offices this week
articles.nri_angle: The Indian-American community's largest-ever Capitol Hill advocacy day — 200 delegates pressing immigration reform and the green-card backlog — paired with lawmakers urging the diaspora to run for office amid rising anti-Hindu and anti-India hate, marks a strategic shift for NRIs from quiet professional success toward direct political representation, with the visa and PR backlog issues that affect millions of Indian families at the centre of the agenda.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Canada Issued Millions of Work Permits. Now They're Expiring — and Indians Are Half the Wave.
articles.excerpt: About 1.4 million permits lapse in Canada this year against just 380,000 permanent-residency slots. The arithmetic doesn't work, and the people it strands are disproportionately Indian.
articles.image_caption: An Air Canada aircraft at the gate. Tens of thousands of Indian work-permit holders face expiry in 2026 amid a permanent-residency backlog.
articles.nri_angle: Indians make up roughly half of Canada's temporary-resident approvals, so the 2026 expiry wave — 1.4 million permits lapsing against just 380,000 PR slots — puts a uniquely large share of Indian students, workers and their spouses at risk of falling out of status or being forced to leave, with knock-on effects for remittances and a talent influx back into India.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: AI's Hunger for Memory Just Made Your Next Phone More Expensive. India Will Feel It Hardest.
articles.excerpt: Memory-chip prices have leapt as much as 89% in a single quarter as AI data centres swallow the supply. Apple is already raising prices — and the world's second-biggest phone market is squarely in the blast radius.
articles.image_caption: Memory modules like these have surged in price as AI data centres absorb global chip supply
articles.nri_angle: India is the world's second-largest smartphone market and overwhelmingly price-sensitive, so the AI-driven 'RAMageddon' memory surge — already forcing Apple and rivals to raise prices — will hit Indian buyers of budget phones and laptops hard, even as Micron's new Sanand plant in Gujarat marks India's bet to climb the semiconductor ladder; NRIs face the same hikes abroad and a longer-term investment story in memory's shift from commodity to strategic asset.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America Has Run Short of a Cancer Drug. It Just Sent an SOS to India's Drugmakers.
articles.excerpt: The US FDA has quietly asked Indian manufacturers to supply ifosfamide — a chemotherapy in short supply after a US plant disruption — a reminder of how much the world's medicine cabinet leans on India.
articles.image_caption: Vials of chemotherapy drugs; the US FDA has asked Indian manufacturers to help supply the cancer drug ifosfamide
articles.nri_angle: An NRI family with a relative in cancer treatment in the US has a direct stake in whether ifosfamide stays on the shelf — and an Indian-made vial may be what fills the gap; the FDA's explicit appeal to Indian drugmakers underscores India's standing as the pharmacy of the world and offers the diaspora both reassurance and a recurring investment angle in names like Cipla, Alkem and Zydus.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Judge Killed Trump's $100,000 H-1B Fee. Two Weeks Later, It's Quietly Back.
articles.excerpt: A Boston court struck down the fee on June 8 as an unlawful tax — then paused its own ruling. USCIS may keep collecting the six-figure charge while the appeal proceeds, and Indians, the largest H-1B group, are again left guessing.
articles.image_caption: A US visa in a passport; a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions is back in effect while a federal appeal proceeds
articles.nri_angle: Indians receive the largest share of H-1B visas, so the on-again, off-again fate of Trump's $100,000 fee — struck down on June 8 but back in force days later while the First Circuit weighs the government's appeal — directly governs whether Indian engineers, doctors and researchers can still realistically be sponsored, and the resulting uncertainty is pushing many toward Canada or a return to India.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: U.N. Halts Strait of Hormuz Evacuation After Cargo Ship Is Attacked, Stranding Thousands of Sailors Again
articles.excerpt: A drone strike on a tanker off Oman forces the IMO to suspend a rescue that had just freed 1,100 seafarers, reviving fears for the fragile U.S.-Iran deal and the Indians who crew the world's ships.
articles.image_caption: A tanker lies at anchor waiting to enter port. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz had begun to recover before Thursday's attack forced the U.N. to pause its evacuation.
articles.nri_angle: India is the world's largest supplier of merchant seafarers, with some 18,000 Indians caught on ships in the Gulf and three already killed; a renewed Hormuz crisis also raises India's oil-import bill and pump prices felt across diaspora families.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America Will Soon Let You Pay $750 to Skip the Visa Line. India's Travellers Are the Obvious Customer.
articles.excerpt: A six-month State Department pilot starting July 1 lets visitor-visa applicants buy an interview within 10 business days — a paid fast lane in a system where Indians have long waited months for a slot.
articles.image_caption: The U.S. Embassy in New Delhi; a new State Department pilot offers Indian travellers faster visa interviews for a fee
articles.nri_angle: Indians generate some of the world's heaviest demand for US visitor visas and have long faced months-long appointment backlogs, so a paid fast lane offering an interview within 10 business days — for USD 750 on top of the USD 185 fee — lands squarely on the diaspora's frequent fliers, from parents visiting grandchildren to founders and professionals shuttling across the India-US corridor.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: After a Decade of Waiting, India's Biggest Stock Exchange Is Finally Going Public. The Owner of the Market Is About to Join It.
articles.excerpt: The National Stock Exchange has filed for a roughly Rs 30,000-crore offer-for-sale — set to be India's largest-ever IPO — at a valuation near $55 billion, ending a listing saga that has dragged since 2016.
articles.image_caption: The National Stock Exchange building in Mumbai; NSE has filed for what would be India's largest-ever IPO
articles.nri_angle: NRIs increasingly route remittances and savings into Indian equities and index funds, and the NSE IPO offers a chance to own a piece of the marketplace itself — a stock that has been off-limits until now — with eligible NRIs able to apply via NRE/NRO portfolio accounts, while the back-to-back NSE and Jio mega-listings signal the deepening of the very markets the diaspora uses to keep financial roots at home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Adani Is Betting $2 Billion That the Next City Grows Around the Airport, Not the Other Way Around
articles.excerpt: The group's airports arm will build 'airport cities' — hotels, offices, retail and entertainment — across more than 655 acres at six Indian airports, modelled on Singapore, Dubai and Amsterdam.
articles.image_caption: An airport terminal in India; Adani Airports plans 'airport cities' across six Indian airports
articles.nri_angle: NRIs experience India most often through its airports, and Adani's $2 billion bet on 'airport cities' at Mumbai, Ahmedabad and four other hubs means more hotels, business space and world-class terminals for diaspora travellers — while reshaping the earnings of a group that is a fixture of NRI investment portfolios directly and through Indian index funds.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: After Three Years of Talks, the India-UK Trade Deal Finally Goes Live July 15 — and It Quietly Rewrites the Rules for Indian Workers Abroad
articles.excerpt: Cheaper Scotch and British cars grab the headlines, but the deal's real prize for the diaspora is a pact that spares some 75,000 Indian professionals from paying into two countries' social-security systems at once.
articles.image_caption: India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal, in London for talks before the India-UK trade deal takes effect July 15
articles.nri_angle: For Britain's 1.9-million-strong Indian community — the country's largest ethnic-minority group — the deal cuts tariffs that touch NRI-run import, restaurant and textile businesses, eases visas for chefs, yoga teachers and musicians, and, most importantly, ends the double social-security charge on the roughly 75,000 Indian professionals seconded to the UK who until now paid into two pension systems while collecting from one.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Twin Earthquakes Devastate Venezuela Near Caracas, Killing Scores — and the Shock Reaches India's Oil Bill
articles.excerpt: Two powerful quakes struck barely 39 seconds apart, flattening buildings in a country already hollowed out by years of crisis, while a jump in crude prices ripples toward import-dependent India.
articles.image_caption: Caracas, Venezuela; twin earthquakes near the capital have left thousands feared dead
articles.nri_angle: A catastrophe in Venezuela reaches Indians on two fronts — the long-rooted Indian-origin communities across the Caribbean and Latin America with relatives and businesses in the region, and the wider economy at home, where a quake-driven rise in global crude prices lifts the import bill of a country that buys more than 85% of its oil abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Financial-Crime Agency Raided the World's Biggest Gold Processor. The Books Allegedly Didn't Match the Vault.
articles.excerpt: After SEBI accused Rajesh Exports of inflating revenue by an almost unimaginable Rs 15.15 lakh crore, investigators found the physical gold was 40% short of what the ledgers claimed — and money trails running to the UAE and African mines that no one can fully account for.
articles.image_caption: Refined gold bars; the ED found Rajesh Exports' physical gold stock about 40% short of its books
articles.nri_angle: Through its Shubh Jewellers chain and the Valcambi refinery — a globally trusted source of minted gold bars and coins — Rajesh Exports sits close to the supply chain NRIs buy from for weddings, festivals and savings, so allegations that a marquee Indian gold name fabricated revenue on a record scale, routed metal through suspicious UAE channels and came up 40% short on physical stock strike directly at the diaspora's confidence in the integrity of Indian gold and in the Indian equities and jewellery brands many of them invest in.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Fire at a Tata Data Centre in Delhi May Have Erased 20 Years of One Company's Data. Google Cloud Was Hit Too.
articles.excerpt: A June 5 blaze at the STT-Tata facility in Greater Kailash caused 'extensive damage,' and three weeks on the recovery is still failing — a warning about how much of digital India sits in a handful of buildings.
articles.image_caption: Server racks inside a data centre; a June 5 fire at the STT-Tata facility in Delhi caused extensive damage
articles.nri_angle: NRIs depend on Indian cloud and telecom infrastructure daily — from international SIMs and remittance apps to the e-governance portals used to renew OCI cards, file taxes and manage NRI accounts — so a Delhi data-centre fire that may have destroyed 20 years of one firm's records and disrupted Google Cloud across India is a direct warning about how concentrated, and how fragile, the digital systems holding diaspora documents and money can be.
